title: A Personal Story Using Phrasal Verbs
writingModel: How I Almost Gave Up English — by Rustam Seilov

In my second year of secondary school, I very nearly gave up learning English. I had been putting off the work for weeks, telling myself I would catch up later. But when the exam finally arrived, I found out that "later" had become "too late." I failed the test and had to sort out a meeting with my teacher to discuss what had gone wrong.

My teacher didn't give me a long lecture. She just asked me one question: "Do you want to carry on?" I said yes, but without much conviction. She told me to come back the next day with a list of everything I didn't understand, and she would go through it with me. I expected her to give up on me. She didn't.

Over the next month, we worked through the grammar together. She set up a simple system: I would write down ten new words each evening, look them up in context, and come up with one sentence for each. It seemed like a lot at first. But I kept at it, and gradually it started to work. I was making progress.

One day I came across an English book in my school library — an old novel with damaged pages. I picked it up, read the first paragraph, and understood almost everything. I went back and read it again just to be sure. I put the book back carefully, went home, and didn't mention it to anyone. But something had changed.

I never looked back. I carried on improving — through films, music, conversations, and eventually university. When I look back now, I realise the turning point wasn't finding out that I had failed the exam. It was finding a teacher who didn't give up on me when I had almost given up on myself.

I sometimes pass on this story to younger students who are struggling with English. "Don't give up," I tell them. "And don't put off the work — it only piles up. Find someone who believes in you and go through the hard parts together. It gets easier. I promise."
